clue.text: Discard half of that egg on seeing crack

indicators.note: throwing away half a word leaves only its other half, here the back two letters

blocks.note: the front half TH is thrown away, leaving the back half
to egg someone on is to urge or entice them

explanation.surface: A cook gives up on a half-used egg once it turns out to be cracked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crack' looks like part of the egg story, but it is the definition, in the sense of 'have a crack at'. 'Egg on' is a phrasal verb, not breakfast.
explanation.definitionFit: To have a crack at something is to make a try at it, so the noun crack is a colloquial synonym.

clue.text: Crafty sea trout, dropping or rising freely

indicators.note: in a down entry something rising reads from the bottom upwards, so the short word turns round
to drop something is to let it fall away, so these letters leave the fish
letters moving freely are not tied to their places, so what remains is rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written, the name of the fish
taken as written and then turned round; this pair sits in the middle of the fish

explanation.surface: An angler admires a cunning sea trout that keeps diving and surfacing at will.
explanation.walkthrough: Removing RO from SEATROUT leaves SEATUT, which rearranges to ASTUTE. 'Dropping or rising' reads like a fish's movement in the water.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone crafty is shrewd and cunning in getting their way, which is what astute describes as an adjective.

clue.text: Bottom place for royal projected broadcast

indicators.note: a broadcast goes out over the air to listeners, so the word is to be heard rather than seen

blocks.note: projected means hurled or thrown

explanation.surface: A royal ranked at the bottom has their image projected on air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bottom' is not a ranking but the part of the body that sits down: the definition is the seat a monarch sits on.
explanation.definitionFit: A throne is the ceremonial chair of a monarch, literally the place where a royal rests their backside.

clue.text: Plug in marquee's animated front

indicators.note: one piece goes in among the other's letters before they are stirred
animated means lively and moving about, so the combined letters are jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written, with the S from the apostrophe
a plug is an advertisement, AD for short

explanation.surface: An advert lights up the front of a marquee with moving signs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Front' looks like the marquee's facade, but it is the definition in its sense of a false show. To plug a product is to advertise it.
explanation.definitionFit: A front is a pretence hiding the truth, and a masquerade is likewise a false outward show or disguise.

clue.text: They'll lay out a fortune to turn traitor over

definitions.note: the definition is plural because the answer names a pack of cards, many items under one singular name

indicators.note: turning something over flips it, so the joined letters are read backwards

blocks.note: taken as written
to rat on someone is to betray them

explanation.surface: Informers who sell out their side are paid a fortune for it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lay out a fortune' sounds like spending a lot of money, but here the cards are laid out on a table to tell a fortune.
explanation.definitionFit: Tarot cards are dealt in a spread by fortune-tellers, who read the future from the pattern on the table.

clue.text: Wind back instalment of virtual art simulation

indicators.note: an instalment is just a part of the whole, so the letters are a run inside the phrase
going back means reading from right to left

blocks.note: the run starts at the end of the first word and stops early in the third

explanation.surface: Someone rewinds an episode of a virtual reality art show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wind back' looks like the rewinding of a recording, but 'Wind' is the definition, the noun for a moving air current.
explanation.definitionFit: The mistral is a strong cold northerly wind that blows down the Rhône valley into southern France.

clue.text: Little snapper bit rolls covered with instant milk

indicators.note: something that rolls over ends up the other way round
in a down entry, being covered means the other pieces sit on top

blocks.note: a mo is a moment, a British short form
to milk a situation is to exploit or use it
a bit is a part

explanation.surface: A small child takes a bite of bread rolls topped with powdered milk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Little snapper' suggests a child or a small fish, but it is a device that snaps shut. 'Bit', 'rolls' and 'instant milk' all read as food.
explanation.definitionFit: A spring-loaded catch for small rodents snaps shut on its victim, so it is a small snapping device.

clue.text: Do a bunk after husband's put down bit of capital

indicators.note: in a down entry, putting a letter down moves it lower, so it is lifted out and slotted further along

blocks.note: doing a bunk is running off; shoo is the call that sends someone off
H is the standard abbreviation for husband, lifted out of its second place

explanation.surface: Someone runs away after a husband has been killed, taking part of the capital.
explanation.walkthrough: The H of SHOO slides one place lower down the entry, after the first O. Soho is a district of central London known for nightlife.
explanation.definitionFit: Soho is one neighbourhood of London's West End, so it is a small part of the capital city.

clue.text: Article from Spain written in secret, revolutionary puts in post again

indicators.note: writing something in puts it inside a text, so one piece goes inside another
a revolution overturns the order of things, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: el is the Spanish word for 'the'
taken as written

explanation.surface: A Spanish revolutionary's article, written in secret, returns someone to office.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Article' looks like a newspaper piece, but it is the grammatical article. 'Revolutionary' reads as a noun for a rebel but is the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Voters who return a sitting official to office for a further term put that person back in post.

clue.text: Tucked into cornflakes, I'd eaten with water at hand

indicators.note: something tucked into a phrase is wrapped up inside it, so the letters run continuously within the words

blocks.note: the letters run straight on from the end of the cereal through the next two words

explanation.surface: Someone describes having had breakfast cereal with water at hand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tucked into' reads as eating, which suits the breakfast picture, but it means the answer is buried in the words. Crossing the comma and apostrophe is allowed.
explanation.definitionFit: A lakeside place lies on the shore of a lake, so there is water close by.

clue.text: Times names relations

blocks.note: first meaning: fixed periods, as in school or prison sentences
second meaning: words used for things, as in technical vocabulary
third meaning: standing between people, as in being on good ones

explanation.surface: The Times newspaper publishes the names of family members.
explanation.walkthrough: This is a triple definition: three separate meanings of one word. The capital T makes the first look like the newspaper.
explanation.definitionFit: The plural noun covers periods of time, vocabulary words, and the footing on which people stand with each other.

clue.text: Model with bit of bottle gets rowdy

blocks.note: a rough is a preliminary sketch or mock-up
the narrow top part of a bottle

explanation.surface: A fashion model who has had a drink or two becomes loud and disorderly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rowdy' reads as an adjective in the surface but is the definition as a noun, a rowdy person. 'Model' means a draft, not a catwalk figure.
explanation.definitionFit: A rowdy is a rough, noisy troublemaker, and a roughneck is an informal term for the same kind of brawling person.

clue.text: Polish perhaps bound to be shrinking

indicators.note: the word signals that the named item is only an example of a wider class

blocks.note: the language of Poland is one example of a tongue
bound means tied up

explanation.surface: A tin of polish that keeps getting smaller as it is used up.
explanation.walkthrough: Capitalised at the start, 'Polish' could be the shine for shoes; it is the nationality, and its language is a tongue. 'Shrinking' means shy, as in a shrinking violet.
explanation.definitionFit: A shrinking person is timid and withdrawn, and someone too shy to speak is described as unable to find words.

clue.text: Sci-fi screening, vacuous Empire Returns 9

definitions.note: the number points to the answer at 9 across, used here in its sense of charges

indicators.note: a vacuous word is empty inside, so only its outside letters remain
a screen shields what is behind it, so one piece wraps round the other
returning means coming back, so the assembled letters are read backwards

blocks.note: SF is the usual abbreviation for science fiction
only the first and last letters are kept

explanation.surface: A cinema shows a science fiction film, a hollow sequel called Empire Returns 9.
explanation.walkthrough: The italic title mimics a Star Wars sequel but carries only wordplay. The 9 is a cross-reference: it points to TERMS, meaning charges here.
explanation.definitionFit: The terms of a deal can mean its charges or prices, as in reasonable rates, and fees are payments charged.

clue.text: Done reading mystery

blocks.note: first meaning: a volume shut when it is finished with
second meaning: something or someone impossible to understand

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests someone has finished a mystery novel; the two parts are separate meanings of one phrase. The first is a literal reading of the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: A person or subject that cannot be understood is idiomatically called this, just as a shut volume cannot be read.

clue.text: Firmly covered up romance, cuddling Romeo – Papa dealt roughly

indicators.note: to cuddle is to wrap one's arms around, so one piece holds another
something done roughly is done without care for order, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: amour is a love affair
Romeo is R in the NATO phonetic alphabet
Papa is P in the NATO phonetic alphabet
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone hushed up an affair with Romeo after Father treated him harshly.
explanation.walkthrough: Romeo and Papa look like a lover and a father in a family drama, but they are just letters of the phonetic alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: Something with a protective steel skin is thickly covered against attack, so heavily shielded describes it.

clue.text: Revolting old boy with debts hanging around Number 10

indicators.note: in a down entry, something hanging around below another piece sits underneath it

blocks.note: OB is the abbreviation for old boy, a former pupil
No. is the abbreviation for number
X is ten in Roman numerals
IOUs are written promises to repay

explanation.surface: A disgusting old boy with debts loiters outside Number 10 Downing Street, the Prime Minister's residence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Number 10' looks like Downing Street but splits into two abbreviations. 'Revolting' reads as rebellious; here it means disgusting.
explanation.definitionFit: Revolting means extremely unpleasant or offensive, and the answer is a common synonym for that adjective.

clue.text: Away days holding black magic seances

indicators.note: to hold something is to contain it, so one letter goes inside
magic transforms things, so the letters are conjured into a new order

blocks.note: B is the abbreviation for black, as on pencils
taken as written

explanation.surface: Trips away are spent holding sessions of black magic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Black magic' reads as a single phrase, but 'black' gives a letter and 'magic' is the signal to rearrange. Away days are days off, not trips.
explanation.definitionFit: Days spent away from work or school are recorded as instances of not being present.

clue.text: Keep in good condition or state

blocks.note: first meaning: look after something so it stays in working order
second meaning: declare or assert that something is so

explanation.walkthrough: 'Condition or state' looks like a pair of synonyms, but 'state' is a verb meaning to assert, and the second definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb covers both servicing equipment to keep it working and insisting firmly that a claim is true.

clue.text: Sort of school exam result that's given to a high-flier?

blocks.note: a school where pupils live in term time
a successful grade in a test

explanation.surface: A top boarding school pupil earns exam results that mark them out as a high-flier.
explanation.walkthrough: A high-flier sounds like a star pupil, but the question mark signals a literal reading: an air passenger flying high.
explanation.definitionFit: Airline passengers are handed this card before getting on the plane, so it is literally given to someone who flies.

clue.text: Muscles stretch out making a climb or quick descent

indicators.note: in a down entry, climbing means going upwards, so the letters read from bottom to top

blocks.note: abs are abdominal muscles
to stretch out on a bed is to lie down

explanation.surface: A climber's muscles get a stretch on the way up or a rapid descent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Climb or quick descent' looks like a pair of alternatives for one activity, but 'making a climb' only turns a piece round.
explanation.definitionFit: Abseiling is a rapid controlled way down a rock face or wall on a rope, so it is a fast descent.

clue.text: Flexible shelter housing a new resident

indicators.note: to house something is to give it a place inside, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: a shelter of canvas, which bends and moves
taken as written
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: A flexible shelter scheme offers housing to a new resident.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Housing a new resident' reads like a landlord's advert, but 'housing' is the container signal. 'Flexible' just describes the soft walls of the shelter.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who rents and lives in a property is its occupier, so a renter is a resident.

clue.text: Twisted heart of Dante's Inferno

indicators.note: the heart is the centre, so the outside letters go and the middle ones stay
twisting something round leaves it facing the other way

blocks.note: the first and last letters of the name with its S are dropped

explanation.surface: A critic calls the core of Dante's Inferno twisted.
explanation.walkthrough: The italic title suggests the poem, but 'Inferno' alone is the definition: a blazing volcano. Etna is the active volcano on Sicily.
explanation.definitionFit: An erupting volcano is a fiery furnace of molten rock, so the word for a blazing fire fits it.

clue.text: Writing item in Echo & Times, tinker half-heartedly – it's throwaway

indicators.note: with half its heart gone, one of the two middle letters is removed
one piece is placed in the middle of the others

blocks.note: Echo is E in the NATO phonetic alphabet
X is the multiplication sign, read as 'times'
a pen is something to write with
to tinker is to dabble, dropping one B of the doubled pair

explanation.surface: Someone dismisses a feature in local papers, the Echo and Times, as half-hearted tinkering fit only for the bin.
explanation.walkthrough: The italic Echo and Times look like newspapers, but they are letters: E from the phonetic alphabet, X as the multiplication sign. The pen sits between them and DABLE.
explanation.definitionFit: Something throwaway can be discarded without loss, which is what an expendable item is.

clue.text: Feelings of discontent with uneven losses mean an audit

definitions.note: the definition is plural but the answer is a mass noun for a state of mind made up of such feelings

indicators.note: losing the uneven, odd-numbered places leaves the even-numbered ones

blocks.note: the second, fourth, sixth, eighth and tenth letters

explanation.surface: Staff grumble that losses on the books will mean an audit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Uneven losses' sounds like patchy financial losses, which fits the audit; it means losing the odd-numbered letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Ennui is a listless weariness and dissatisfaction from boredom, a kind of discontent.

clue.text: Funny item showing edge Mirror ultimately edited out

indicators.note: ultimately means at the end, so only the final letter is used
something edited out is cut from the text, so a letter is removed

blocks.note: to skirt is to go round the edge; a skirt is a border or fringe
the last letter of the word

explanation.surface: A comic piece in the Mirror newspaper was cut by the editor at the last minute.
explanation.walkthrough: The italic Mirror looks like the tabloid newspaper, but only its last letter matters.
explanation.definitionFit: A skit is a short comic sketch or parody, so it is a humorous piece of entertainment.

clue.text: Ending of blue joke delivered in the wrong order

indicators.note: the two pieces are given the other way round from how the clue lists them

blocks.note: a crack is a wisecrack
feeling blue is feeling low

explanation.surface: A comedian fluffs the punchline of a dirty joke by telling it backwards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blue joke' looks like a smutty gag, but the two words are separate pieces. 'Ending' is the definition, not part of the joke.
explanation.definitionFit: A crackdown is firm action to stop an activity, bringing it to an end, so it is a stamping out.

clue.text: Homeric character, nothing great

blocks.note: the letter O looks like a zero
mega is slang for great or excellent

explanation.surface: A reviewer finds a figure from Homer's epics unremarkable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Homeric character' suggests Achilles or Odysseus, but character means a letter: Homer wrote in Greek.
explanation.definitionFit: Omega is the last letter of the Greek alphabet, the script Homer's epics are written in.

clue.text: Jolly, spinning the Devil's music

definitions.note: the definition is a mass noun while the answer is plural, but several pieces together are music

indicators.note: a spinning thing turns round, so the letters face the other way

blocks.note: jolly is British for very, as in jolly good, and so is very
the Devil's name

explanation.surface: Someone cheerfully plays the devil's music on a turntable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jolly' looks like an adjective for merry but works as the British adverb meaning very. The 's after Devil joins it to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Sonatas are classical compositions for one or two instruments, so together they are pieces of music.

clue.text: Dark psychological profile?

blocks.note: surface reading: a grim assessment of someone's character
setter's reading: a black shape used in a personality test, as in the Rorschach test

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase suggests a sinister criminal profile, but the question mark points to a literal dark mark used to probe the mind.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Rorschach test patients describe what they see in symmetrical dark stains, revealing their personality.
